Headlinne · brand system v4 · Aug 2026

It passes 19,210 checks. Here is the draft.

30 seconds, encoded to MP4, narration that flows the way you would explain it. A CTA close that changes pose every day. And a runthrough that renders all 720 frames and checks them — it caught four real bugs, including the overlap you spotted.

The two things you said made the SpaceX story good — it applies to everyone and it's uplifting — are now weighted terms in the ranker. They changed the whole list.

01 — Selection

You named the two missing criteria

"It applies to everyone, and it's uplifting." I added both as weighted terms and re-ran against live feeds. Same 208 stories, same gate, same minute as yesterday's run.

Every one of those is universal, concrete and genuinely worth knowing. The moon story now holds three of the top five. Yesterday's run — before these two terms — had the Taliban anniversary at number one and an eclipse observatory above the moon crash.

How the two terms work

TermWeightRewardsPenalises
Universal2.6Moon, brain, ocean, sleep, energy, climate, phone — things every human has a stake inCouncil, constituency, earnings, quarterly, FTSE, by-election, midfielder
Uplift1.8Discovered, breakthrough, recovering, restored, solved, milestone, repair—

The trade you're making, stated plainly

Weighting universality pushed "Afghan women tell the BBC their lives are unrecognisable" out of the top eight. That story matters. A news product that never covers Afghanistan because it isn't universal has a real problem, and I don't want to hand you a ranker that quietly does that.

Keep universality as a tilt, not a filter. Reserve one slot a day for a story that's important without being universal, chosen by score within the non-universal pool. One line of code, and it stops the feed becoming all wonder and no world.

02 — Register

Informational, and interesting because of it

You were right that Pip had drifted chatty. He explains now. The interest lives in the facts, not the delivery.

Too informal — the old script

"Okay. Something hit the Moon."

"Nobody meant to do it."

"Here's my favourite part."

"Oh."

Informational — the new one

"On Tuesday a four-tonne rocket stage struck the Moon."

"Solar activity pulled it off course."

"Energy equal to three tonnes of TNT."

"It was reported as SpaceX. It was a Chinese Long March 3C."

Same warmth, no jokes. Pip's personality now shows through what he chooses to tell you and in what order — which is a more durable kind of character than a catchphrase, and it can't go stale.

A four-tonne rocket hitting the Moon does not need help being interesting.

03 — The reel

30 seconds, and it explains rather than announces

Rewritten to flow the way you described it out loud — “it was up there because solar activity pulled it off course, so it released energy equal to three tonnes of TNT.” Because, and, which, so. One thought, not eleven headlines.

The draft, looping · 540×960 · 30s

Two reading budgets, not one

You were right that the detail line does not need reading word for word — it supports the reader rather than competing with them. So the runthrough now measures two rates: 176 wpm on the primary line (ceiling 230, the readable limit) and 288 wpm total on-screen load (ceiling 380, scanning speed).

Measuring them as one block gave 308 wpm and would have forced a rewrite you did not want. The pace you liked is unchanged.

The bubble picks its side

Pip walks the full width, so a bubble pinned to his right runs off the frame by the time he reaches the CTA. It now measures the room on each side, sits on whichever has space, clamps to the margins, and mirrors its tail so it still points at him.

The runthrough missed this because I had never traced the bubble. Tracing it immediately surfaced a second, older problem: the bubble was tucked ten pixels over Pip’s shoulder and had been overlapping him on every frame it appeared. Both fixed — 19,806 assertions now, still zero failures.

The sign-off differs every time

Pip jumps, presents, points, walks or talks on the CTA — rotated deterministically by day, the same trick hooks.py uses so a month of posts never collapses into one look.

The band below y=1450

Still deliberately empty. Instagram’s caption block, handle, audio strip and action rail sit exactly there — anything drawn into it is covered in the feed. Everything from the masthead to the source strip now occupies 180–1440 with no dead band inside it.

04 — Runthrough

19,806 assertions, zero failures

qa.py renders every one of the 720 frames and checks them the way a reviewer would, but on all of them. It has found six real bugs so far — two of them only after I widened what it watches.

FoundFix
The overlap you spotted. On the counter beat the detail line was pinned to a fixed y and collided with the main line.Detail now positions from wherever the line actually ended, with a floor above the source strip.
The second plate ran off the canvas — right edge at 543px on a 540px frame, for 40 straight frames.Both plates clamp inside the margins, and shrink when there are two.
Marigold failed contrast at 2.72:1 on paper, below even the large-text floor of 3.0.Darkened to #946217, now 4.65:1, changed everywhere it is used.
Point, present and talk never moved — one pixel of travel, and a beak opening changes no bounding box at all.Three frames each with real travel. The check now compares pixels, not bounding boxes.

That last one was also a bug in the checker. A test that cannot see the thing it is testing passes while the product is broken. Same reason the contrast test now imports the real colour constants instead of re-typing them — it was still checking the old marigold after I had already replaced it everywhere else.

What it checks

  • No two elements overlap, on any frame
  • Nothing renders below y=1450, outside the margins, or above the masthead
  • Every accent clears its contrast floor on paper
  • Every sprite pose renders non-empty; every animation cycle actually changes pixels
  • All four rungs of the fallback ladder produce a real object
  • Both pace budgets hold, and no beat outruns its reading time
  • The CTA exists in all three formats and varies at least four ways
  • Every static card is the right size and is not 98% one colour

05 — Rate limits & cadence

Keep two reels a day — but change how speech is called

You asked me to check before committing. Text is nowhere near a limit. Speech is the binding constraint, and the current design makes it far tighter than it needs to be.

Your own config already documents it: the free tier allows three speech requests per minute, one call is made per beat plus the sign-off, and calls are spaced 21 seconds apart to survive that. My script has eleven beats — so two reels is roughly 24 speech calls a day, up from the fourteen your comment was written around, and about eight minutes of deliberate waiting per run.

One call per reel, not one per beat. Twenty-four a day becomes two.

Request the whole narration in a single call, take the one PCM stream, and scale the beat timings to its measured duration. normalise_durations() in motion.py already distributes time proportionally — it just needs the real total instead of a per-clip measurement.

The trade: you lose per-beat audio boundaries, so sync comes from word-count proportions rather than measured clips. For kinetic text that is imperceptible — it would only matter if you were lip-syncing. What you gain is roughly a twelvefold drop in speech quota, which is the difference between two reels a day being tight and being trivial.

Add a text fallback chain

REEL_TTS_FALLBACK_MODELS already exists and the reasoning behind it is right: quota is counted per model, so a second model is a second allowance. GEMINI_MODEL has no such chain. Mirror it.

SettingValueWhy
GEMINI_MODELgemini-3.1-flash-liteCurrent primary
GEMINI_FALLBACK_MODELSgemini-3.1-flash,
gemini-2.5-flash-lite,
gemini-2.5-flash		Each is a separate daily allowance
On a 429advance immediatelyThe rule you already wrote for speech: do not wait out a window you cannot use

The new cadence

FormatWasNowCost per item
Reels2 / day2 / day1 text + 1 speech call, after the batching change
Story card1 / day1–2 / day1 text call
Carousel1–2 / day1–2 / week1 text call

That is roughly five or six text calls and two speech calls a day — 22 to 30 posts a week with enormous headroom. Set IG_SECOND_CAROUSEL=false and gate the carousel behind a weekday check.

So: keep two reels a day. If you would rather not touch the speech batching yet, drop to one reel a day until you do — twelve calls is survivable, twenty-four is not.

Check the quota page before trusting any of this

The per-model numbers in circulation — 15 requests a minute and 1,000 a day for flash-lite, 10 and 250 for flash — come from third-party trackers rather than Google, and free-tier quotas were cut in December 2025. The shape of the argument holds regardless (speech is the constraint, batching fixes it, per-model chains multiply the allowance), but verify the actual numbers on the official quota page before you tune the spacing.

04 — Plates & fallbacks

Tilt it, tape it, and always have the next rung ready

A straight rectangle reads as a screenshot. A tilted one reads as an object — paper frame, 3° rotation, soft drop shadow, a strip of masking tape.

The ladder

Every rung is a designed object. None of them is a bare gradient.

RungWhenWhat renders
1The article has a usable imageThe photo, tilted in a paper frame with tape and a source caption
2No image, but the category has a sceneA generated pixel scene — captioned ILLUSTRATION · NOT A PHOTOGRAPH, always
3No image, but the story has figuresA generated chart plate from the numbers in the article
4Nothing usable at allPip presenting the headline. No plate, larger type, more air

The caption is not optional

A generated scene must carry ILLUSTRATION · NOT A PHOTOGRAPH every single time it renders. You are building a brand on the claim that you show your working — shipping a drawn crater that a reader could mistake for a NASA image would undo more trust in one post than the receipt bar builds in a month. Put the caption in the plate function, not in the caller, so it cannot be forgotten.

Every other fallback

WhenFallback
Fewer than 2 independent sourcesDo not publish. Gate, not a penalty.
Story is sensitive (death, disaster)Sober template. No Pip, no bubble, no kinetic emphasis, no wonder framing.
Headline needs more than 3 linesRoute to carousel. Never shrink the type.
No number in the storySkip the counter beat entirely rather than inventing a stat.
Sources disagreePip puzzled, both figures shown, resolution in the caption.
Requested pose unavailableFall back to idle. Never render an empty sprite slot.
Script exceeds 220 wpmAssertion fails the build. Cut words, don't shorten holds.

05 — X

The card carries the proof, never the headline

1200×675. On X the post text is the hook — so the image must add something, not repeat. Your current cards duplicate the headline in both and waste the strongest position on the platform.

The correction card is the one to lead with. It's a format no single-outlet account can run, it's visually unmistakable, and it makes the argument for the product without a word of marketing. Post the claim as text, reply with the card.

Thread shape

  • Post 1 — the claim, as plain text. No image. "Reuters says 12,000 jobs. The FT says 4,000. Same memo."
  • Post 2 — the compare card. Showing your working doubles the surface area.
  • Post 3 — the resolution. "One counted contractors." This is the post that gets quoted.

Keep the investment here small. 15% of under-25s use X for news against 42% on Instagram — X earns volume and replies, not bespoke art. All four cards reuse components you already built.

Order

  • Ranker first. It changes every post forever; everything else changes how posts look. Add the reserved non-universal slot at the same time.
  • Wonder feeds second. Phys.org, Space.com, New Scientist, ScienceDaily all fetched cleanly. Four of the new top eight come from feeds you don't have.
  • Plates before Pip. The fallback ladder is what stops a bad image day producing a bad post, and it's independent of the character.
  • Then Pip, the reel, and X.

Two things I'd still check before shipping: re-verify the moon facts against Al Jazeera and Space.com directly rather than my paraphrase, and run interest.py on a slow news day. Today had a genuinely good story in it — the ranker deserves a test on a dull morning.
